newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Giant Russian plants say Ukraine alumina ties sour.
newsitem.headline: Giant Russian plants say Ukraine alumina ties sour.

text.p: Two giant Russian aluminium smelters have broken off talks with Ukraine's biggest alumina supplier as relations between the two sides took a turn for the worst, senior Russian officials said on Thursday.

The Siberian Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk smelters said that the Mykolayiv alumina plant in southern Ukraine was asking for too much money, and that they would seek raw material suppliers outside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

"Unfortunately we cannot agree on the price, and their (Mykolayiv's) price is higher than world prices," Yuri Shlaifshtein, a board member at the world's largest aluminium smelter Bratsk, told Reuters.
"We say now we will buy alumina outside the CIS. There it is much cheaper," said Gennady Druzhinin, board chairman at Krasnoyarsk, the world's second biggest plant.
Alumina is a raw material used in producing refined aluminium.

Shlaifshtein said the gap between buyer and seller was between $35 and $40 per tonne, but would not elaborate on outright prices. He said Mykolayiv's prices were inflated by high production costs and an overall lack of competitiveness.
But he also said Bratsk may renew talks in March.
"We do not plan to renew negoatiations before the beginning of March," he said.
Druzhinin said that the break-down in discussions between the two sides was costing his plant money.
"We are losing money, because abroad the price of alumina is rising," he added.
Prices have firmed lately to around $185/190 a tonne, fob Australia, from $140/145 in the third quarter last year, Macquarie Equities said in a recent report.
Russia, chronically short of supplies of alumina, has been seeking supply contracts from the Mykolayiv plant with an eye to securing nearby raw materials at low prices.
Both Bratsk and Kransonyarsk said that they have covered most of their alumina requirements for 1997, although some purchases still need to be made.
It takes about two tonnes of alumina to make one tonne of aluminium. In 1996 Bratsk produced 783,000 tonnes of refined aluminium and Krasnoyarsk 777,000 tonnes.
"We still have some shortfalls. Out of around 1.5 million tonnes of alumina (for 1997), we still need 30,000 to 40,000 tonnes," Krasnoyarsk's Druzhinin said.
"We have basically covered our needs (for 1997)," Bratsk's Shlaifshtein added.
Last month Mykolayiv's deputy commercial director, Hennady Bushtruk, said that the plant planned to sell 90 percent of its 1997 output to Russia, but that no contracts had been signed.
But Shlaifshtien said that Mikolayiv could well struggle to find buyers for its annual alumina production of around one million tonnes if Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk pulled out.
"It is not difficult to imagine that without sales to Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk, the plant could be on the verge of stopping (production)," he said.
Russian aluminium industry sources said that Mykolayiv had 18,000 tonnes of unsold alumina on the plant premises which it was unable to sell.
"A lot of loaded (train) wagons are waiting to go, but it has not been sold...there are no buyers," said one source, who declined to be named.
Druzhinin said that Krasnoyarsk was looking to boost alumina output at the troubled Achinsk plant to 700-750,000 tonnes this year to help secure raw materials for the smelter in the future.
